title: Restaurant Kitchens as Chefs for Small Care Homes
one_liner: License a turnkey program that lets restaurants use dead hours to cook dietitian-approved, texture-modified meals for 6-20 bed assisted-living and adult-family homes that big foodservice ignores.
customer: Operators of small licensed residential care homes (adult family homes, board-and-care, personal care homes, small RCFEs) pay per resident per day, typically $8-12 for lunch and dinner. Adult children pay for premium 'chef-cooked' upgrades. The restaurant is the supplier, and the platform takes a license fee and revenue share.
problem: In a small care home, food is the main daily pleasure and the top resident complaint, yet it is cooked by overworked caregivers from warehouse-club and broadline food, with little variety and hard-to-manage special diets (mechanical soft, pureed, low-sodium, diabetic). Sodexo and Compass do not serve 6-bed homes and meals-on-wheels serves people at home. Meanwhile my kitchens sit idle from 2 to 5pm and on slow days, my cooks want more hours, and my dine-in traffic is soft.
solution: A meal program in a box for restaurants: a rotating 5-week menu library with dietitian sign-off and texture-modified variants (IDDSI levels), allergen and diet labels, batch-cook and cook-chill (or same-day hot delivery) SOPs, a state-specific health-department pre-clearance checklist and HACCP plan templates, routing and billing software, and a contracted registered dietitian on retainer. The restaurant cooks in dead hours and delivers 2-3 times a week in labeled pans, and the care home reheats. Ten homes at about $17-22k per year each is $170-220k of found revenue at healthy contribution margin on capacity that was previously idle.
why_now: The 65+ population is growing fast (the 'Peak 65' wave runs through about 2027). Families are shifting to small, cheaper residential homes rather than large assisted-living campuses. Restaurant dine-in traffic has been soft and owners are actively looking for non-traffic revenue. Kitchen labor is short, and steady off-peak hours help retention. Public state license lists make the small-home buyer easy to find. I couldn't verify current home counts this session, so pull the licensing-list counts state by state before building.
revenue_model: Onboarding fee of $1-2k per restaurant, plus 10-15% of meal revenue, plus software billing at about $100 per month per restaurant. Optional premium tier for adult-child paid 'chef upgrades' and dietitian services.
non_obvious_insight: The gold is in the mismatch between an idle asset and an ignored customer. Small-home operators are often immigrant nurses and caregivers running a tiny business with no procurement power, and no large foodservice company will serve them, but a two-location restaurant can absorb a 300-meal-per-week route into dead hours at nearly zero marginal labor cost. What a restaurant cannot do alone is the compliance layer (texture modification, diet labeling, dietitian review, regulator pre-clearance), and that is the product.
first_30_days: Pull the state's public list of small residential care homes and shortlist 30 within a 15-minute drive. Call my health department to confirm what is required to supply prepared meals from a licensed restaurant to a licensed facility. Hire a freelance registered dietitian by the hour for one 2-week menu. Offer 3 homes a free trial week, then convert them at about $9 per resident per day. Document the SOPs and the regulator's answer as the first version of the product.

title: Menu Trial Lab: Restaurants as Food-Brand Test Sites
one_liner: A network of two-to-five-unit restaurants that run randomized menu experiments for food brands and commodity boards, and get paid for it.
customer: Emerging food and beverage brands (sauces, blended or alternative proteins, beverages), commodity checkoff boards (beef, pork, dairy, potato, avocado and similar), and distributor private-label teams pay $10-25k per trial. Independent operators are paid a fee and free product and get menu-engineering results back.
problem: Foodservice launches fail because the operator's ROI is unproven, not because guests dislike the item. Line speed, storage, training, plate cost and cannibalization decide whether an item survives. Brands pay for sales reps, menu-placement deals and consumer surveys, but survey data measures stated preference. The item then sits in my walk-in. Reps tell operators 'it sells' with no data to prove it.
solution: Recruit a network of 2-5-unit independents who connect Toast, Square or Clover. Each trial is a randomized matched-pair test: the item is on the menu at one location and not at its twin, then swapped, and we run a difference-in-differences on attach rate, check average, cannibalization, plate cost and contribution margin per cover. The deliverable is a 'Menu Adoption Scorecard' plus an operator-facing ROI one-pager the brand's reps and distributors can use to close accounts. Automated matched-pair design and automated POS reading keep unit costs low.
why_now: Beef, coffee, cocoa and dairy cost pressure has kept operators reformulating (blends, substitutions) since 2025, and brands need proof under tighter budgets. POS platform APIs and partner ecosystems now make continuous read access practical at scale. AI makes experiment design and reporting cheap. Commodity boards and distributors are under pressure to show operator-level ROI. I could not verify whether an existing network already sells this, so check Datassential, Technomic and distributor pilot programs first.
revenue_model: Fee per trial ($10-25k) paid by the brand or board, with a portion (say $500-2,000) paid to each participating operator. Later, annual data subscriptions for brand teams and 'scorecard' licensing to distributors.
non_obvious_insight: A two-location owner is a natural experimenter, since it is the only cheap way to run a true A/B with identical kitchens, menus and staff. Nobody in food innovation uses that. The buyer's real question is 'will an operator make money and keep it on the menu', which no consumer panel answers. The moat is the operator network and their POS data, not the analytics.
first_30_days: Post in owner Facebook groups and a regional restaurant association to recruit 10 two-to-five-unit operators, including my own two locations as pilot sites. Approach 5 emerging brands at a regional foodservice show with a $5-8k, four-week matched-pair trial. Run my first trial in my own two restaurants and turn the results into a 3-page scorecard to use as the sales collateral for the next brand.

title: Contingency Water-Bill Recovery for Small Commercial Sites
one_liner: A no-win-no-fee service that rebuilds small commercial sites' water, sewer and stormwater bills from the local tariff and claws back irrigation-sewer overcharges, leak credits and stormwater-fee errors.
customer: Owner-operators of small multi-tenant commercial properties (strip centers, 20-200 unit apartment communities, self-storage), churches, private schools and nurseries in cities that bill sewer on metered water and charge stormwater fees. Start in one drought metro. Referral partners are their bookkeepers and property managers.
problem: A $5k-$40k/yr water bill is too small for utility-audit firms, who chase national chains, and too tangled for the bookkeeper, who codes it and pays it. Tariffs sit in council resolutions. Scarcity tiers and surcharges keep changing. Sewer is often billed on metered water that includes landscape water that never reaches the sewer. Stormwater fees rest on impervious-area estimates that are often wrong. Leak-adjustment windows lapse unnoticed. The Fed's 2026 small-business survey names rising costs the #1 financial challenge.
solution: The owner forwards bills or connects QuickBooks/Xero and the utility portal. An LLM pipeline reads the tariff PDF and rebuilds every bill. It flags misclassified meters, irrigation on sewered meters, overnight-flow leak periods in interval data, impervious-area disputes (checked against aerial imagery) and estimated reads. A human analyst files the credit, refund or reclassification with the utility, chases it to cash, and writes corrected coding back into the books. Wedge product: an 'irrigation-sewer plus stormwater credit audit' for one metro and three utilities.
why_now: 49.6% of the US was in drought on Sept 24, 2026 after the warmest June-August on record, so scarcity pricing and surcharges are multiplying. Regulated private water companies invested about $6.8B in 2025 ($43.5B over the decade) and recover it through rate cases that small customers never see. LLMs make it cheap to read hundreds of heterogeneous tariffs and bills. Customer portals increasingly expose interval meter data. Intuit and Xero are rebuilding around LLM subscriptions and cannot easily take contingency fees.
revenue_model: 30% of verified first-year savings plus recovered refunds (contingency). Then a $25/site/month monitoring plan that stops corrections regressing and catches new leak periods. White-label for property managers at about $8/door/year.
non_obvious_insight: The one-time refund is the hook, not the product. The value is the permanent reclassification of the account (meter class, irrigation split, impervious area), which lowers every future bill. The moat is a tariff library that human auditors cannot afford to build for accounts this small. Outcome-priced work does not fit subscription incumbents, so the real competitor is nobody.
first_30_days: Pick one metro with a published stormwater-credit manual and an irrigation or deduct-meter option. Hand-collect five utilities' tariffs. Recruit 20 owners through the local apartment association or BOMA chapter and 5 bookkeepers who get a 10% referral. Audit 24 months of bills per site with the LLM pipeline plus one analyst, with no upfront fee. Targets: 10 audits by day 30, first 3 recovered checks by day 60, then publish anonymized results as the sales asset.

title: Courthouse-Handwriting Graph to Clear Heirs' Property
one_liner: Use AI that can read old handwritten deeds and probate files to map who really owns family land that never went through probate, and sell clean title to the buyers who need it.
customer: Solar, wind, pipeline and broadband developers, land trusts and conservation buyers, timber and ag buyers, and title insurers, with legal-aid partners protecting heirs.
problem: When a landowner dies without probate, title fragments among dozens of heirs. Developers can't lease or buy without consent, and heirs can lose land through partition sales. The records are handwritten across probate, deed and marriage files, so clearing one parcel takes lawyers weeks or months.
solution: LLM handwriting recognition over courthouse records builds a family-of-record graph per parcel, ranks probable heirs, finds them, and manages consent, lease or purchase packages through e-signature. Partner attorneys file quiet-title or partition actions for hard cases. Developers get a 'title-readiness score' per parcel. The design bakes in fair terms and legal aid for heirs.
why_now: Multimodal models now read historical cursive at near-human accuracy, and county records are increasingly scanned. The Uniform Partition of Heirs Property Act has been adopted in a couple dozen states, which pushes toward consensual deals. The land rush for solar and data-center sites needs clean title fast.
revenue_model: $2K-$10K per cleared parcel paid by the developer or a percentage of lease value, plus data licensing to title insurers.
non_obvious_insight: The transfer that never went through probate, family land passed informally for generations, is a hidden inventory of blocked assets. Now a buyer with money (energy and data infrastructure) will pay to clear it.
first_30_days: Pick one county in a solar-active area with high heirs' property prevalence. Get a developer's list of blocked parcels. Process 10 parcels and partner with a heirs' property legal clinic to review the process and heir outreach.

title: Impersonation Firewall at the Distributor Gate
one_liner: A KYC-style API that distributors call before publishing a release under an existing artist name, so one upstream check protects every streaming service at once.
customer: Mid-size self-serve music distributors and label-service companies, which carry the upload volume, the DSP penalties and the legal heat from labels. Estates and small catalogs benefit downstream.
problem: Everyone treats DSP-side approval as the fix, such as Spotify's Artist Profile Protection beta (Mar 24, 2026) and its verified badges (Apr 30). But impersonation enters through distributors, which sit upstream of every DSP. The brief cites Sony's 135,000+ removal requests, and AI tracks were pushed onto pages of Jeff Tweedy, Father John Misty and the late Blaze Foley in Aug 2025. Spotify's protection only helps artists who opt in, on one service.
solution: An API that scores each new release in seconds. It checks (1) name and identifier collisions against existing artist pages on public DSP APIs, (2) proof of control over the claimed identity through handle-linking challenges and a short liveness video for unknown names, and (3) audio-embedding similarity between the new master and the claimed artist's catalog. Suspicious releases go to a human review queue with an evidence pack. It returns allow, hold or reject, and every decision is logged.
why_now: Platform policing arrived (Spotify beta, TIDAL, Bandcamp) but only at the shelf, not the door. Deezer reports AI above 50% of uploads, so distributors face rising takedown and fine volume. AI-powered impersonation is now cheap.
revenue_model: $0.10-0.40 per release check with a $1-3k/month minimum, plus review-queue seats and a premium tier for auto-holding high-risk releases.
non_obvious_insight: The platforms sell AI tools themselves and each protects only its own pages. The distributor is the only place where cost, liability and the payout relationship line up, and a KYC check there is cheap compared with cleanup after upload.
first_30_days: Build a prototype on public Spotify, Deezer and Apple search APIs plus open audio embeddings. Back-test it on the documented impersonation cases. Offer 10 mid-size distributors a free retro-audit of their last 90 days of releases, and convert one or two into a paid pilot.

title: Claims Desk for Government-Paid Childcare
one_liner: A medical-billing-style revenue-cycle service that turns small providers' attendance sheets into clean subsidy and universal-program claims and advances the cash within 48 hours.
customer: Family child care homes and one-to-three-site centers in states and cities with subsidy or universal-care programs, such as NYC and New Mexico (the latter from memory).
problem: As governments become the payer (universal-care promises, 2026 tax credits, tighter CCDF rules), providers face attendance logs, eligibility recertification, claim rejections, 30-60 day payment delays and fraud audits. Margins are thin, payroll is about 70% of cost, and the average worker earns $33,140. Home providers, the fastest-growing segment at +4.3%, have no back office.
solution: Providers send attendance photos or export from Brightwheel, Procare or Kangarootime. The service validates against each program's rules, fixes errors, submits claims and chases denials. It then offers advances against verified claims, funded by a partner lender. A running library of each state's rejection codes drives the automation.
why_now: Subsidy-fraud scrutiny and attendance-verification demands rose sharply in winter 2025-26 (from memory, not verified in the brief). Universal or free-care programs are launching and the DCFSA and 45F expansions add spending. Payment-rule changes reward providers who can document cleanly.
revenue_model: 3-5% of collected subsidy revenue plus a 1.5-3% factoring fee on advances. Payroll-timing savings make it an easy sell.
non_obvious_insight: Healthcare RCM became a giant industry because the payer changed. Childcare is going through the same payer shift with no RCM industry yet. The moat is knowing each state's rejection codes and quirks, which a services-plus-software firm accumulates claim by claim.
first_30_days: Pick one state with slow, public-rule subsidy payments. Recruit 10 home providers via Facebook provider groups and the local CCR&R. Do the claims by hand with one ops hire and a spreadsheet at 4%. Log every rejection reason. Add advances through a small-business lender partner in month 2.

title: Disordered-Eating Tripwire for GLP-1 Prescribers
one_liner: A cheap, documented eating-disorder screen and escalation network embedded in GLP-1 telehealth intake.
customer: White-label medical groups that supply prescribers to many telehealth brands, GLP-1 telehealths, med spas and their malpractice carriers.
problem: GLP-1 use was ~50% among binge-eating-disorder patients and ~42% among atypical anorexia patients (JAMA Psychiatry 2026), and an NEJM 2026 perspective warned about masking and worsening disordered eating in telehealth. An investigation tied four white-label medical groups to ~30% of telehealth firms receiving FDA warning letters, and MDL 3094 has 4,700+ cases pending. Plaintiff lawyers and boards look for the next vector, and no screening or monitoring layer exists.
solution: A 3-minute validated screen (SCOFF or EDE-Q short form) inside intake, 2-question monthly check-ins, rules-based escalation to a network of ED-trained dietitians and therapists, and an exportable audit trail for boards and insurers.
why_now: FDA sent 30 letters in Mar 2026 and 25 in Jun 2026. Regulators, boards and carriers are moving to documented safeguards. The data showing high GLP-1 use in eating-disorder populations is new in 2026.
revenue_model: $3-6 per screened patient, $40-80 per escalation (paid by the prescriber or referral network), and a malpractice-carrier discount program.
non_obvious_insight: In white-label telehealth, liability concentrates in the medical group that sits behind dozens of brands, so a cheap, documented safeguard is standard-of-care insurance. ED providers also need referral flow, so escalation pays for itself.
first_30_days: Pitch two mid-size white-label groups or a 20k-patient telehealth. Deliver via an embeddable link, run 500 screens, and publish flag-rate benchmarks. Recruit 10 ED-trained clinicians for escalation.

title: Unstaffed Overnight ICU for Vet Clinics
one_liner: Radar-based contactless vitals and camera analytics let general practices keep IV-fluid and post-op patients overnight without a 24-hour staff, easing ER transfers and ER overload.
customer: 2-10 DVM general practices and low-cost clinics with a small treatment ward, plus shelter medical wards such as parvo units.
problem: With about 2 techs per vet, most clinics cannot staff nights, so hospitalized pets are transferred to 24-hour ERs at higher cost, sent home early or not treated. That drives owner cost, client loss and ER crowding.
solution: A low-cost mmWave radar puck per cage measures respiratory rate and motion, with a camera to watch IV lines and pumps. An on-site alert plus a pooled remote overnight RVT/DVM desk cover 20 clinics, with thresholds tuned by species and weight.
why_now: Consumer sleep-tracking made mmWave sensors cheap, edge vision models run on small devices, the tech shortage is structural, and the spectrum-of-care movement wants intermediate options between full transfer and no treatment.
revenue_model: $150 per cage hardware plus $79-149 per cage per month, and per-night remote-coverage fees.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone tries to automate diagnosis. The binding constraint is night hours: the lack of an awake person forces a general practice to hand revenue and clients to the ER. Monitoring substitutes for staying awake, not for the doctor.
first_30_days: Buy off-the-shelf radar and cameras and instrument 4 cages in 2 friendly clinics. Log respiratory-rate accuracy against manual counts for 30 nights. Sell $99-per-cage pilots and recruit pooled overnight RVT coverage.

title: School Deepfake-Nude Incident Response Retainer
one_liner: A 24/7 retainer that walks school districts through the first 72 hours of an AI-generated nude incident: hash-based takedowns, evidence handling, reporting duties and parent communications.
customer: School districts, charter networks and independent schools. Channel: school risk pools, cyber and liability insurers and brokers.
problem: Nudify apps let anyone turn a student photo into sexual imagery. Schools improvise: staff viewing the images can itself be illegal, mandated-reporting and Title IX duties are unclear, and takedowns must be filed on many platforms. The federal TAKE IT DOWN Act (2025) requires platforms to remove reported intimate imagery within 48 hours, with platform compliance due May 2026 (from memory), but victims and schools don't know the process.
solution: A playbook plus tooling: secure intake that hashes images without staff viewing them (StopNCII and NCMEC Take It Down style), pre-filled takedown requests, a state-by-state legal duty checklist, evidence logs, communication templates for parents and students, and counselor referral. A retained hotline handles live incidents.
why_now: The TAKE IT DOWN Act's platform obligations kicked in this year, incidents are proliferating, and insurers are re-underwriting districts for cyber and child-safety exposure.
revenue_model: $3-12k annual retainer per district, per-incident fees, and bundle or referral deals with insurers and school risk pools.
non_obvious_insight: The worst thing a school can do is look at the evidence, so the product is a don't-look-just-hash workflow. Insurers are the channel because one mishandled incident costs far more than the retainer.
first_30_days: Draft the playbook with a school-law attorney and a former juvenile detective. Pitch 3 school-insurance brokers or state school-board risk pools. Run free tabletop exercises for 5 districts. Convert the best relationship into the first paid retainer.

title: Install-and-Map Crew for Crowdfunded Yard Robots
one_liner: A local white-glove setup and seasonal-care service for the $4-5K yard robots that Kickstarter backers are buying and struggling to get working.
customer: Owners of $2,200-$5,500 crowdfunded or prosumer yard robots (Yarbo M and similar): affluent suburban homeowners with 0.5-2 acres, seniors who cannot lift a 200 lb unit, and small landscaping and snow-removal firms. Payer is the homeowner or firm, with an installer-referral fee from manufacturers or resellers as a later option.
problem: Big-ticket crowdfunded robots ship as a Shenzhen-supported product that takes multiple weekends to set up: RTK antenna placement, GPS calibration, yard mapping, no-go zones, firmware chasing. It weighs about 200 lb, and owners report escalations without resolution from a China-based support team.
solution: A certified two-person install crew that does a one-visit RTK site survey (satellite-visibility check, antenna mounting), lifts and assembles the unit, maps the yard, sets zones and snow paths, and hands off with a 30-day check-in. Add a $19/mo seasonal-care plan covering firmware updates, blade and attachment swaps, and pre-winter snow-blower setup. Start with Yarbo, then extend to other $3K+ crowdfunded home robots and ultra-short-throw laser projectors (5,260 backers took the $2,999 XGIMI tier).
why_now: Yarbo M backers were told to expect delivery from August 2026, and snow-blower-module backers ship mid-November, right before the season the module exists for. That gives a hard deadline in autumn 2026. Wire-free RTK robots are only now cheap enough for homeowners, and the seniors and heavy-yard buyers who most need help are exactly the ones who cannot self-install.
revenue_model: $399-$799 per install visit (higher for wooded or complex lots), $19/mo or $149/yr seasonal-care plan, and $99-$199 per attachment swap or spring/fall visit. Optional B2B contracts for landscapers converting to robot fleets.
non_obvious_insight: The Kickstarter tech median pledge is $194, but this robot's backers average over $4,000 each ($3,158,140 from 751 backers, https://www.gizmocrowd.com/post/yarbo-m-yard-robot). At that price the buyer is effectively a serviced-equipment customer, not a gadget hobbyist. Hands-on reviews say setup took multiple weekends, the unit weighs about 200 lb (owners "could not have set the unit up alone"), GPS struggles under tree cover, support runs from China with East Coast friction, and the maker declined Home Assistant API access in March 2025 (https://seekandscore.com/yarbo-review/). Crowdfunded hardware makers optimise for shipping units, not last-mile success, so the installer layer is unowned. It is a local-services business with software-like repeat revenue.
first_30_days: Read public Kickstarter and Yarbo forum comments to find backers in snow-belt ZIP codes, and post in the Yarbo owner communities offering a founding-customer $299 install. Recruit 2-3 landscapers or handymen who already own a truck and lift gear. Run 5 paid installs on your own or friends' properties to write a mapping and RTK-survey checklist, then film one before/after case study. Book 15-20 installs timed to the November snow-blower shipments and sign one landscaping firm to a pilot contract.

title: Stomach-Ready: GLP-1 Protocols for Endoscopy Centers
one_liner: An intake, coaching and point-of-care gastric ultrasound service that stops GLP-1 patients from turning up to endoscopy with a full stomach and getting cancelled on the table.
customer: Independent GI practices and ambulatory surgery centers (ASCs) that run 5-30 endoscopies a day, plus anesthesia groups that staff them. The buyer is the medical director or administrator.
problem: GLP-1 drugs slow gastric emptying. Studies in 2026 show retained gastric contents in roughly one in five endoscopy patients on the drugs, and some procedures are aborted. Guidance has moved from 'stop the drug for a week' to 'continue it, use a 24-hour clear-liquid diet, do selective gastric ultrasound and communicate across teams'. Centers have no operations layer to run this. Front-desk staff cannot tell who is on which drug, at what dose or when the last injection was. Surprises happen day-of, causing cancelled slots, rebooking, extra anesthesia risk and idle rooms.
solution: A text and portal intake flags GLP-1 users (brand, dose, weekly or daily, last injection date, symptoms). It auto-assigns the guideline-based protocol, sends coaching and adjusts dose timing per the clinician's rules. It flags high-risk patients (dose escalation phase, gastroparesis symptoms) for a 90-second gastric POCUS on the day. A travelling RN sonographer or a trained center nurse does the scan with a handheld device, and the result goes straight into the anesthesia record. Phase 2 adds AI-assisted image reading.
why_now: A April 2026 wave of studies (residual gastric content 'far higher than expected') and updated multi-society guidance made continue-and-modify the new standard, which needs new workflows. Oral Wegovy and orforglipron are about to widen the user base. Procedure centers are squeezed on throughput and cannot afford dark rooms.
revenue_model: $15-30 per GLP-1 patient screened and coached, plus $60-100 per gastric ultrasound performed. Alternatively a flat $500-1,500 per site per month. One avoided aborted case is worth roughly $1k+ in recovered slot revenue.
non_obvious_insight: The expensive problem is not the rare aspiration event, it is aborted cases and scheduling chaos. Guidelines supplied a protocol but nobody supplies the operations layer that knows which day of the week each patient injects. The physician societies are a free distribution channel once a protocol is written up.
first_30_days: Get 2-3 GI ASCs on a free 60-day pilot and measure their baseline aborted and rebooked rate. Have a GI and an anesthesiologist advisor sign off on a protocol drawn from published guidance. Build the intake on Twilio and a simple form. Buy two handheld ultrasound units (about $3-5k each) and contract an RN sonographer for spot coverage. Then convert the pilot sites to paid.

title: Sworn Testator Depositions for the Deepfake Era
one_liner: Estate attorneys refer aging or blended-family clients to a 45-minute sworn Q&A on intent and capacity, taken by a reporter who certifies it and stored in an escrow vault that opens on death. Because a human certified it, it stays credible when video can be faked.
customer: Estate planning and elder law attorneys, whose clients pay $1,200-$3,000 per session (billed through as a cost). Also wealth advisors and family offices serving blended-family, dementia-risk or high-conflict heirs. Trust and estate litigators are a secondary buyer.
problem: The great wealth transfer is driving more will and trust contests over capacity and undue influence. The standard defense is a video of the signing, but anyone can now claim video or audio is synthetic or edited. Attorney file notes look self-serving, and witness memory fades over the 5-15 years between signing and death. Court reporters are the one neutral officer who can administer an oath and certify a verbatim record. Only litigation agencies dispatch reporters, so estate lawyers never think to hire one.
solution: A productized package. A licensed reporter administers the oath. The attorney or an independent examiner runs a structured interview covering assets, family, reasons for unequal splits, and awareness of who might object. An optional treating-physician attestation is added. The client receives a certified transcript, hash-locked and time-stamped video, and the reporter's certificate. Everything goes into an encrypted escrow vault that releases on a death certificate or an attorney trigger. Clients re-sit every 2-3 years. The package maps to ante-mortem probate options in the few states that have them (Ohio and Alaska are examples) and to each state's rules for perpetuating testimony. Admissibility varies by jurisdiction, so attorneys own the legal strategy.
why_now: Deepfakes are making courts wary of unauthenticated audio and video. The federal Advisory Committee on Evidence Rules was still working on a Rule 901(c) deepfake amendment and a new Rule 707 for machine-generated evidence at its October 2026 meeting. Remote depositions and remote-reporting laws such as California's AB 3013 make flexible scheduling normal, and estate sessions can be scheduled unlike litigation work. The wealth transfer is under way now.
revenue_model: $1,200-$3,000 per session, with about 50-60% going to the reporter. Vault fee of about $150 per year. $600 re-sit sessions every 2-3 years, which creates a recurring long tail. No referral fees to attorneys, because ethics rules prohibit fee splitting. Attorneys bill the session as a case cost.
non_obvious_insight: The reporter's certificate and oath are the one part of a transcript AI cannot counterfeit, and its value rises as media authenticity falls. Estate planners sit outside the reporter dispatch network, so nobody has packaged the reporter's authority for them.
first_30_days: Partner with 2 licensed reporters and 1 estate attorney, ideally in a large metro or an ante-mortem-probate state. Write the interview protocol with the attorney and a geriatric psychiatrist consultant. Offer a free pilot to 10 estate and elder-law firms through bar CLE lunches and local ACTEC chapters, targeting one blended-family client each. Aim for 5 paid sessions by day 30.

title: Warm-Backup Servicer for Orphaned Solar
one_liner: Be the standby operations-and-maintenance contractor for lenders and securitization trustees holding portfolios of systems whose installer died.
customer: Trustees and servicers of solar loan and lease securitizations, tax-equity and debt holders, and buyers of distressed portfolios. Homeowners can buy direct as a secondary channel.
problem: Sunnova, Titan, ADT Solar and Freedom Forever failed. Manufacturer warranties survive but nobody supplies the service labor, and monitoring clouds die. Customers with dead inverters stop paying, which erodes the cash flows lenders depend on.
solution: A backup-servicing contract. Onboard the portfolio's asset data, replace dead monitoring clouds with a local gateway, dispatch vetted local technicians through a roll-up network, handle manufacturer RMA and warranty claims, and upsell battery retrofit and VPP enrollment.
why_now: The bankruptcy wave of 2024-26 has portfolios sitting in trustees' hands. With 25D gone there are fewer new installers. A 46% storage attach rate means more complex systems in the field.
revenue_model: $8-15 per system-month standby retainer, a $250-450 margin per truck roll, an RMA handling fee, and referral fees for battery and VPP enrollments.
non_obvious_insight: Lenders do not care about kilowatts. They care about payments, and a homeowner with a dead inverter stops paying. Service is a credit-protection product, and its buyer is the party with the balance sheet and the pain.
first_30_days: Identify three distressed portfolios from trustee reports and call the servicers. Sign a 1,000-system pilot in one metro. Onboard two local service shops. Build the gateway on vendor APIs and local Modbus.

title: Blinded Diligence Bureau for AI-Biotech Financiers
one_liner: A buyer-paid, blinded prospective testing service that tells pharma BD teams, royalty funds and lenders whether an AI drug-discovery platform's claims hold up in a neutral wet lab.
customer: Pharma BD&L and search-and-evaluation teams, corporate VCs, venture lenders, synthetic-royalty funds and crossover investors underwriting AI biotechs.
problem: AI-biotech capital is enormous ($6B+ in 2026, including Isomorphic's $2.1B and Chai's $400M). Deals are headlined in biobucks: Genentech-Earendil is $55M upfront against $1.5B+ total. Buyers still rely on vendor-supplied retrospective slides. The public competitions (Adaptyv, Anthropic x Adaptyv) test protein binding only and are public, not confidential diligence on a buyer's own targets. Small-molecule, antibody and ADMET claims have no neutral test.
solution: A custom blinded bake-off. The buyer picks 5-20 targets or properties (binding, potency, developability, ADMET). Two to four shortlisted vendors submit designs under NDA. Neutral partner labs assay them blind: an Adaptyv-style lab for binders, a CRO for ADMET. The buyer gets a ranked result, hit rate versus controls, a free open-model baseline (Boltz, BindCraft and similar) and a red-flag memo. Vendors never pay for ranking.
why_now: Frontier-lab designs hit about 27% in Adaptyv's blind test (1,320 designs, 16 targets, 354 binders), so 'does it beat free open models' is now the right question. Software-only AI shops are wobbling (Schrodinger cut staff), and mega-rounds attract generalist money that cannot judge the science. At least 12 funded biotechs sold for $1B+ this year, so acquirers need fast technical diligence. Adaptyv just raised $40M, so neutral wet-lab capacity can be rented.
revenue_model: $60-250k per blinded engagement, $150k/year retainers for funds that see 10+ platforms, and anonymized aggregate 'state of AI design' reports as a secondary product.
non_obvious_insight: 'Beats a free open-source baseline' is the question nobody prices. Buyer-paid independence, with no vendor fees, is the only credible model. Neutral labs already exist to rent, and consultancies lack lab access. Competitions such as Adaptyv's are partners and lead sources, not rivals, because they are public and binder-only.
first_30_days: Pitch 5 corporate-VC and BD teams currently evaluating platforms and sign 2 pilots at $40-60k. Rent capacity from an Adaptyv-style lab and one CRO. Design a 10-target panel with 3 anonymized vendors plus an open-model baseline. Publish the methodology to build trust.

title: Mother-Tongue Lifeline for Dementia Flashpoints
one_liner: On-demand live video calls where a dementia-trained speaker of the patient's first language and dialect coaches the English-speaking aide and calms the patient at bath, bedtime and exit-seeking moments.
customer: Home care agencies and PACE programs in immigrant-dense metros (NYC, LA, Miami, Chicago, Bay Area, Houston) with dementia clients whose aides do not share their language. Second: Medicaid managed long-term care and D-SNP plans. Third: families on a flat monthly plan.
problem: Bilingual and multilingual patients lose their second language as dementia advances and drift back to the language, dialect and idioms of their childhood. Agencies send whoever is available. The English-speaking aide cannot say the one calming phrase during the bath, so the bath fails, the patient panics, the aide gets hurt or quits, and the family blames the agency. Telephone interpretation lines translate literally, but a dementia patient's fragments and proverbs need to be validated, not translated. It is a communication problem, not an interpretation problem.
solution: A dedicated line, staffed on demand by trained bilingual retirees, nurses and teachers, covering the long tail: Yiddish, Haitian Creole, Toisanese, Cantonese, Polish, Russian, Uzbek, Punjabi, Tagalog, Greek, Armenian. A tablet or phone is propped where the patient can see it. The specialist speaks to the patient in dialect while coaching the aide in English in the earpiece: 'she's asking for her sister, say she is coming, then hum this song.' Sessions are 3-10 minutes at known flashpoints. Specialists are trained by aides in validation and redirection, not interpretation.
why_now: The post-war Soviet, Chinese, Caribbean and Southeast Asian immigrant cohorts who arrived in the 1960s-80s are now reaching moderate-to-severe dementia. Low-latency video is universal and cheap. AI companions such as KindredMind (voice clone of the caregiver, 12 languages, launched worldwide in May 2026) prove the demand, but they work best for mild cases and comfortable tech users. For moderate-to-severe dementia and live crises, the warm human voice in the right village dialect is the missing complement, and the agencies will pay per minute for it.
revenue_model: $1.25-1.75 per minute billed to agencies and plans, with 60-70 percent gross margin after specialist pay of about $0.45 per minute. Families get $129 per month for 20 sessions. Later, enterprise contracts with MLTC and D-SNP plans that cover the cost as a quality tool.
non_obvious_insight: Patients revert not just to a language but to a specific dialect and era, for example Toisanese, not Mandarin, and the idioms of 1955. A literal interpreter is useless because what calms is tone, a lullaby, a proverb and a familiar name. The buyer is not the family but the agency, which is desperate because language mismatch is why its aides quit its hardest cases. Nobody pays interpreters for companionship, so this talent pool of bilingual retirees is unmined and cheap.
first_30_days: Pick two languages with dense local demand, for example Toisanese or Cantonese in NYC and Haitian Creole in Miami. Recruit 10 bilingual retirees through churches, senior centers and community media. Train them in a one-page validation script. Run it on WhatsApp video with no software. Call 15 small agencies serving those communities and offer 30 free minutes per case. Sign the first three at $1.50 per minute with a $300 monthly minimum.

title: Licensed Local-Language Speech Data Exchange
one_liner: Pay radio stations and call centers for rights-cleared audio and resell it to the voice-AI builders who cannot get it anywhere else.
customer: Voice-AI startups and model labs that need low-resource African and Indian language audio; radio stations and telco call centers are the suppliers.
problem: Foreign APIs are unusable for local voice because of latency and jitter. Startups like AethexAI train small models on call-center recordings and radio audio, but rights, cleaning and transcription are ad hoc.
solution: A consented, speaker-anonymised and transcribed archive with clear licences and revenue share for stations. The wedge is 3-5 stations in one language (Hausa, Yoruba or Swahili), with a sample set for a paying pilot.
why_now: 300M-1.7B parameter voice models now work in production, and Intron covers 57 languages. Labs face scrutiny over scraped data, and Sarvam and AethexAI are raising money.
revenue_model: $20-80 per cleaned, licensed hour, with 40-50% shared with the station, plus annual subscriptions.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders assume low-resource data is unsellable because the markets are poor. The buyers are well-funded labs, and rights-cleared audio, not raw audio, is the bottleneck.
first_30_days: Sign three stations, digitise about 2,000 hours and clean 200 as a sample. Sell a paid pilot dataset to one voice-AI startup.

title: Thermal Commons on Failed Golf Courses
one_liner: Turn shuttered golf courses into shared geothermal borefields that heat and cool the neighborhoods that already surround them.
customer: Gas and electric utilities running thermal-energy-network pilots, housing authorities and multifamily or 55+ community owners next to a course, and the course owner as a land-lease seller.
problem: Networked geothermal works, but it is starved for land. Dense neighborhoods have no room for borefields, so pilots dig up streets or use scraps of parking lots. Meanwhile ~90 golf courses close a year, leaving 100-150 acre owners stuck in expensive rezoning fights with neighbors who hate new housing.
solution: A small developer that (1) screens closed and for-sale courses by distance to heat loads (apartments, schools, 55+ communities) and utility franchise, (2) options the best sites, (3) runs thermal response tests, (4) designs a borefield and neighborhood loop, and (5) sells capacity to the utility or thermal service to buildings under long contracts. The surface stays green as a public park or trails, which turns a NIMBY fight into an amenity and speeds approvals.
why_now: Utility pilots are real and funded. Eversource's Framingham phase 2 has a $7.8M DOE grant with construction in 2026 and launch in early 2027. NYSEG's UTEN pilot in Ithaca and National Grid's Massachusetts approvals add to that. State thermal-network mandates are spreading, and the utility model is still being written, so a site-finder-and-developer has room to define it.
revenue_model: Phase 1 (first six months): paid feasibility and site-screening reports for utilities, cities and housing authorities ($25-80k each, often grant-funded) plus land option fees. Phase 2: own or co-own the borefield asset with availability payments from a utility, or per-building thermal service contracts over 20 years.
non_obvious_insight: Land, not technology, is the bottleneck, and a failed golf course arrives pre-cleared, flat, surrounded by customers and owned by someone losing money. A borefield leaves the surface untouched, so the same acreage can also be the park that gets you the permit. The pitch to a utility is 'we bring you a community-approved site, not a science project'.
first_30_days: Build a GIS screen of ~500 closed or listed courses against multifamily density and utility service areas in states with thermal-network programs (NY, MA, CO, MD, MN, WA). Send data packs on the top 10 sites to utility pilot teams and housing authorities. Land one paid feasibility study and sign two cheap options ($5-20k each).

title: Insurer-Funded Chronic Care for Diabetic Pets
one_liner: A tech-led diabetes and kidney-disease program for insured pets, paid per member per month by insurers who capture the avoided ER claims.
customer: Mid-size pet insurers and MGAs (for example Fetch, Pumpkin, Odie and Lassie-type carriers) that need to cut claim severity. Independent clinics are the referral partner, and self-pay owners are the fallback.
problem: Diabetes and kidney disease in cats and dogs generate $3-6K a year in claims and emergency DKA admissions. AAHA's 2026 guidelines emphasize CGMs and once-daily insulins, but the workflow of monitoring, titration, coaching and refills has no owner. Vets are overloaded, vet techs are 2 per vet against a 4:1 ideal, and insurers' premiums are up 19.7% against animals up 9%, so they need to reduce claim costs rather than only raise prices.
solution: Sell insurers a PMPM disease-management pod: CGM starter kit, weekly data review by licensed vet techs under a supervising vet via the owner's clinic, protocol-driven insulin titration messages, refill logistics, and early-warning routing to the clinic before DKA. Enrollment is found in the insurer's claims file. Clinics are paid a titration-visit fee so they are not disintermediated. Insurers pay $40-70 PMPM with shared savings on avoided ER events.
why_now: AAHA split canine and feline diabetes guidelines in 2026 and put CGMs at the center. CGMs and long-acting insulins are arriving at once. Ambient AI and the vet-tech underuse make labor arbitrage possible. Insurers face repricing backlash, and remote VCPR rules are loosening piecemeal.
revenue_model: PMPM from insurers, gain-share on avoided claims, and CGM sensor and supply margin. Owner self-pay at $59 a month as a fallback.
non_obvious_insight: Insurers sit on the only longitudinal dataset and carry the financial downside. Clinics hold the license but not the time. This is Livongo-style economics: the payer who owns the downside pays for prevention, and vet techs are the labor arbitrage. Chronic care is a claims-cost product, not a telehealth product.
first_30_days: Convince one small MGA to share a de-identified diabetic-claims cohort and pilot a 200-pet program at cost. Recruit two RVTs and a supervising vet. If insurers are slow, launch a $59 a month owner-pay version through 5 clinics to get outcome data within 90-120 days.

title: Landowner-Side Broker for Data-Center Land
one_liner: A conflict-free advocate that scores your parcel's power value and runs a competitive process, so the family farm isn't sold cheap to an anonymous LLC.
customer: Family landowners with 100-2,000 acres near high-voltage transmission lines or substations, in data-center-active counties, who are getting unsolicited offers. Each deal is worth $5-50M or more.
problem: Developers approach landowners through shell LLCs and landmen, with NDAs and options that lock the land up cheaply. Landowners can't tell whether $30K or $300K an acre is fair, because value now depends on grid interconnection position, water and fiber rather than acreage. Regional brokers don't know how to value power, so owners either sell too low or refuse offers that are actually good.
solution: A licensed landowner-side brokerage. A Parcel Power Score built from public transmission and substation data, utility large-load tariffs, zoning and moratorium status, water and fiber proximity, and an independent power engineer's review. It runs a competitive process to many site-selection teams and developers, negotiates terms (sale, option, lease, JV, decommissioning bonds), and represents only the seller.
why_now: Land purchases for future data centers reached about $6B in the first half of 2026, up roughly 79% from a year earlier (Avison Young), and sale offers in some places run up to 10 times agricultural value. Sept 2026 coverage shows farmers getting huge offers alongside a local backlash and moratoria that make timing and zoning risk decisive. The seller-side infrastructure has not caught up.
revenue_model: $5-15K representation retainer that is credited against a 1-2% success fee. On $10-50M deals this is $100-500K per closing. Optional fee for a second-opinion review of an existing offer.
non_obvious_insight: Land in this market is priced on power queue position, not soil. Buyers know it and sellers don't, and that information gap is the fee pool. Being seller-only and publishing the methodology makes you the trusted party for landowners and gives hyperscalers a pre-assembled, pre-screened pipeline they will actually prefer. The parcel data is a compounding asset.
first_30_days: Pick a cluster of counties around a substation or 345kV corridor in a data-center-active area (for example Ohio, Indiana, Georgia, Texas or Pennsylvania). Build parcel maps with public HIFLD and county data. Mail or door-knock 300 landowners with a free Parcel Power Score. Partner with a rural land attorney and an independent power engineer, get a broker license or partner with a licensed broker, and aim to sign 3 exclusive representation agreements. Send a one-page buyer package to 20 site-selection teams.

title: Paid Exit Capture: Layoffs Become Agent Evals
one_liner: Pay departing employees a completion bonus to turn their tacit exception-handling know-how into the eval sets and edge-case playbooks the employer's AI agents need, before that knowledge walks out.
customer: Head of AI, COO or CHRO at 1,000-20,000-person companies running AI-justified headcount cuts in ops-heavy functions (claims, support, finance ops, procurement), plus PE operating partners doing portfolio-wide cuts.
problem: Companies cut the people who know the long tail, then find their agents fail on it. Reversals are now reported (Klarna rehiring humans in 2025, Commonwealth Bank of Australia reversing 45 cuts, CNBC's Jul 2026 'regret' headline). Exit interviews are HR theatre, and angry leavers have no reason to document anything.
solution: A 2-3 week 'capture sprint' inside the notice or severance window. A consented, paid interview agent plus a domain reviewer walks each person through their 50 hardest cases. Output is a graded eval set (inputs, gold decisions, rubrics, 'when I'd escalate') and a playbook the employer owns. Workers get a bonus scaled to eval quality (measured by held-out agent accuracy), a signed contribution credential and optionally a recall or contract-rights clause.
why_now: AI was the top-cited layoff reason in Challenger data for five straight months through Jul 2026, and enterprise agent rollouts are now bottlenecked by evals and edge cases rather than by models. Reversal stories are giving CFOs a fresh fear. Interview agents are cheap enough to run the sprints at scale.
revenue_model: $15-40k fixed fee per role-cluster capture sprint (roughly $1.5-4k per captured employee after bonuses), plus an annual eval-refresh retainer once the agent is live.
non_obvious_insight: To the employer a laid-off worker is a depreciating liability, but for the agent rollout they are the only source of ground truth on the long tail. You can only get it by paying, and paying on eval quality fixes the incentive. The data is worth far more than the severance delta.
first_30_days: Use public WARN filings to list 40 companies mid-layoff and pitch 15 HR/AI leads a free 5-person pilot at cost. Have an employment lawyer draft the consent, IP-assignment and NDA carve-out template. Deliver one eval set and show before/after agent accuracy as the case study.

title: Turn Half-Empty School Wings Into Child Care
one_liner: A turnkey operator that leases empty classrooms in half-empty Title I elementary schools and runs licensed infant, toddler and before/after-school care in them.
customer: School districts that lease the space (landlord side). Revenue comes from parents (including those on state child-care subsidies), state pre-K funds, and employers or the district itself buying slots for staff.
problem: Birth-rate decline has left many elementary schools 20 to 40 percent empty, and districts are closing buildings. Yet the neighborhood has no infant care, teachers quit over child care, and before/after-school waitlists run for months. Empty rooms cost the district no visible money, so nobody champions them, and district counsel treats a sublease as a liability risk.
solution: Sell a feasibility and licensing audit ($5k to $15k) covering egress, restrooms, square footage per child, fencing, a separate entrance, and the fire marshal. Then operate the program as a license-holding subtenant. Staff it with cross-trained paras and neighborhood parents. Accept subsidy vouchers and state pre-K slots. Give priority to school staff and Title I families, and keep before- and after-school care in the same building. The district gets rent plus a utilities share, and the operator keeps a thin margin.
why_now: Enrollment declines and school-closure fights are peaking. The 2025 tax law raised the employer child-care tax credit starting in 2026, which helps districts and employers underwrite staff slots. Several states are expanding subsidized or universal child care. Federal after-school funding uncertainty in 2025 also opened a gap for paid programs.
revenue_model: Tuition and subsidy revenue for the operator. One-time feasibility and licensing fees. Optional management fee if a nonprofit or district holds the license.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone talks about reusing closed schools. The money is in schools that stay open but are half-empty, where a wing can be subleased tomorrow with no rezoning. Elementary buildings already meet many child-care code items: kid-height restrooms, exits, a playground and a kitchen. The principal knows this from living in the building. The blocker is the district's lease template and its fear of liability, and both are solvable with paperwork.
first_30_days: Map licensing rules in one state and find a nonprofit child-care operator willing to hold the license. Pitch 5 superintendents and principals with a two-page space-utilization audit and a sample lease. Sell three $5k feasibility audits to fund the pilot, and use waitlists from existing before/after-school programs as proof of demand.

title: AI Chat-History Exposure Assessments for Breach Counsel
one_liner: When infostealers grab employees' AI sessions, tell breach counsel what the attacker could actually have read and whether notification is triggered.
customer: Incident-response boutiques, privacy and breach law firms, cyber-insurer panel vendors, and enterprise DPOs. Priced per incident.
problem: Infostealer logs exposed AI sessions tied to 80,000+ corporate domains, and 358 of 482 large companies analyzed had stolen ChatGPT/OpenAI sessions. A stolen session is a searchable archive of contracts, source code, and personal data, and it bypasses MFA. IR tooling was built for mailboxes and file shares, so nobody can say whether an AI-history breach triggers legal notification.
solution: Ingest infostealer-feed hits mapped to employee AI accounts. Combine them with the customer's enterprise export or compliance-API data to classify the sampled chats after the theft window by data class (PII, PHI, credentials, deal information, source code). Deliver a notification-decision memo, an affected-person list, remediation steps (session revocation, key rotation), and an insurer-ready timeline.
why_now: The 2026 infostealer data shows stolen AI sessions at scale. Enterprise AI adoption now puts sensitive work in chat, and insurers are adding AI exclusions, so they want scoping evidence before paying.
revenue_model: $5-25K per incident, with $1-2K per month monitoring retainers and channel referral fees.
non_obvious_insight: The breach is not the stolen cookie but the content behind it, and notification law turns on data, not credentials. No tool in the IR stack handles AI transcripts, so a small team can own the category before platform vendors bother.
first_30_days: Sign 3 IR boutiques as channel partners. Build a classification pipeline over enterprise chat exports. Run the first paid assessments at a $7.5K flat fee using hits from commercial infostealer-intel feeds.

title: Satiety Peptides for Small-Portion Foods
one_liner: Screen food-grade peptides that trigger the body's own GLP-1 release and put them in high-protein snacks.
customer: Protein bar, yogurt and snack brands serving GLP-1 users and people coming off the drugs.
problem: Small-portion products leave consumers unsatisfied, and CPG incumbents lack anything that helps portions feel sufficient.
solution: ML-screened protein hydrolysate peptides verified in enteroendocrine cell assays for GLP-1 secretion, supplied as an ingredient with structure-function claims only.
why_now: About 12% of Americans use GLP-1s, snack volume is shifting, and AI peptide prediction plus cheap CRO assays let a small team screen quickly.
revenue_model: Ingredient supply and licensing with per-kg pricing and development fees.
non_obvious_insight: GLP-1 drugs created a mass vocabulary for satiety, so food can compete at the margins of lower-dose and post-drug users without making any drug claim.
first_30_days: Hydrolyze two cheap protein streams, run an in vitro GLP-1 secretion assay through a CRO, and sample results to five snack brands.

title: Diaspora-Financed Home Batteries for Family Back Home
one_liner: Sell home battery and solar systems to migrants in the US, UK, Canada and EU as a monthly subscription that keeps the lights on for their relatives, underwritten on the sender's credit rather than the recipient's.
customer: Diaspora professionals (Nigerian, Ghanaian, Kenyan, Filipino, Nepali, Bangladeshi) who already fund fuel, diesel and generator repairs for relatives, with installers in the origin city as fulfilment partners.
problem: Families in Lagos, Accra, Nairobi or Manila face daily outages and spend remittance money on diesel and petrol for generators. Local households are unbankable for asset finance, USD lenders carry FX and default risk, and pay-as-you-go schemes collect tiny local-currency payments. The Hormuz shock has raised fuel costs and put about $50bn of Gulf remittances at risk.
solution: A subscription sold in USD, GBP or CAD. A vetted local installer fits a 5 kWh LFP battery plus hybrid inverter (and optional panels) at the relative's home, the sender pays by card over 24-36 months, and ownership transfers at the end. Underwriting uses the sender's developed-market credit profile. A shared app shows the sender live uptime and savings, and the family gets a simple power ledger. On default, the fallback is remote throttling or redeployment of the unit.
why_now: Stationary battery prices fell 45% in a year and Africa already imports more battery dollars than panels. Felix shows migrant payments can run over chat apps at $8B scale. The US 1% tax on cash-funded remittances pushes senders toward card-funded rails (buying goods and services delivered abroad is not a remittance transfer, subject to legal review), and Nigeria and Kenya are opening rules for digital-dollar settlement.
revenue_model: Hardware margin of 15-25% plus a financing spread (about 18-25% effective APR), installer referral fees, and insurance and extended-warranty attach. Dollar collections match dollar-denominated hardware and DFI debt, removing the FX mismatch.
non_obvious_insight: Credit risk is being priced on the wrong person. The one who effectively pays for the outage today is the diaspora sender, through diesel money, and that person has a credit file, a card and hard-currency income. The caregiving motive should also produce lower churn than pay-as-you-go.
first_30_days: Put up a landing page taking $500 refundable deposits through 3-5 Nigerian, Ghanaian or Kenyan diaspora WhatsApp, church and alumni groups. Contract one Lagos or Nairobi installer and ship 20 systems. Use uptime screenshots and family videos for the referral flywheel, and fund working capital from deposits plus a small angel or DFI debt line.

title: Preflight Lab for Steam Frame Verified
one_liner: A shared hardware lab that runs your build on real Steam Frame, Steam Machine and Deck units, finds why it would fail Valve's compatibility review, and fixes it.
customer: Back-catalog publishers with 20-200 older titles, and mid-size indie studios that want the 'Great on Frame' or Steam Machine badge. They pay $250-1,500 per title for preflight plus fix, or $1-3k a month for catalog coverage.
problem: The Steam Frame is an ARM device that runs x86 games through FEX and Proton, and it launched in mid-September 2026. Only about 131 titles were Verified at launch out of tens of thousands. Valve's review is a queue with terse pass/fail notes, and each resubmission costs weeks. Failures are usually boring: launcher windows, first-run dialogs, 32-bit dependencies, cutscene codecs, kernel anti-cheat, controller glyphs, unreadable text, missing the 30fps at 720p floor. Devs can't justify buying a $1,059 headset to test.
solution: A rack of real devices with an automated runner. It launches the build through Steam, drives it with synthetic controller input, and records frame-times. It OCRs UI text height, uses a vision model to catch launcher and dialog windows, and checks the checklist Valve publishes. The output is a ranked punch-list. A paid fix-it tier handles launch options, Steam Input configs, codec swaps and small patches, then resubmits to Valve.
why_now: Steam Machine (June 29, 2026) and Steam Frame (September 2026) just shipped, with FEX and the verified-badge process brand new. The first 6-12 months of a new Valve platform are when badges are scarce and the store gives them the most weight, as happened with Deck Verified in 2022. Back-catalog publishers will want to opt in whole catalogs at once.
revenue_model: Per-title preflight and fix fees, catalog subscriptions for publishers, and a success-based 'Verified or partial refund' premium tier.
non_obvious_insight: The failures repeat across titles, so a publisher with 60 games amortizes every fix, and a lab that has fixed one FMV codec problem fixes it for a hundred games. Studios also can't afford the hardware, so shared capex becomes their opex. Triage by expected Frame-owner overlap, because the badge only pays off in genres that owners actually buy.
first_30_days: Buy 2 Frames, 1 Machine and 1 Deck (about $3.5-4k). Run 10 free preflights for devs recruited from Steam Frame and Deck communities and Linux gaming press. Publish 'the top 10 reasons Frame review fails', drawn from those real runs. Pitch 5 ports and back-catalog publishers a fixed price per title for a 20-title pilot.
